title: Called gently by the blanket he was wrapped in.
subtitle: A tender address before a heavy task
then: This came in the earliest days of the mission in Makkah. Ibn Abbas said it means {idea}O you who are asleep{/idea}, and Qatadah said, the one wrapped in his garments. Allah calls the Prophet ﷺ by the very blanket around him, then asks him to stand.
now: It is late. You are under the duvet with your phone, tired from a long week. Nobody is angry with you. {idea}You are simply being called by name, exactly where you are.{/idea} The first step to rising is being seen as you are.
old: Allah only calls me when I have already got my act together.
new: The call reaches me under the blanket, as I am, and invites me up.
try: Tonight, before sleeping, sit up in bed for one minute and say: here I am, my Lord.

title: Stand through the night, all but a little.
subtitle: The night as training ground
then: Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to leave his covering and stand in prayer at night. The surah introduction explains this was {idea}training for the heavy burden of Prophethood{/idea}. Aishah said the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions stood for a whole year until their feet swelled.
now: Athletes wake at five to train while others sleep. Students stay up before the exam. {idea}The hours nobody sees are where strength is made.{/idea} The night is not only for scrolling until the eyes close.
old: Night is just the gap between one busy day and the next.
new: Night is where the heart is trained for what the day will ask of it.
try: Set an alarm ten minutes before Fajr tomorrow and spend them in quiet prayer.

title: Half the night, or a little less.
subtitle: A measure with room to breathe
then: Ibn Kathir explains that half the night was set instead of the whole night. A little less or a little more, he says, {reward}there is no hardship on you{/reward} in that slight change. Even the first command carried room inside it.
now: You planned to read for an hour and only managed forty minutes. So you call the whole evening a failure and stop. {idea}The measure Allah gives has give in it.{/idea} Less than perfect still counts.
old: If I cannot do the full amount, there is no point starting.
new: Allah set a measure with room in it, so a little less is still a real offering.
try: Pick one worship habit you dropped for being too big. Restart it at half size today.

title: Read it slowly, letting every word land.
subtitle: Tartil: recitation that is not a race
then: Umm Salamah said he ﷺ {idea}paused in his recitation, verse by verse{/idea}. Ibn Masud warned against rushing it like poetry: stop at its amazing parts, and {trap}do not make reaching the end of the chapter your concern{/trap}.
now: Ramadan, and you are racing to finish the juz before bed, eyes on the page count in the corner. {trap}Speed reading, heart elsewhere.{/trap} One verse read slowly, with a pause after it, can do more than ten pages skimmed.
old: The more pages I get through, the better my reading.
new: The Quran is read well when it is read slowly enough to move the heart.
try: Read just three verses today, pausing after each one for one slow breath.

title: A heavy word is coming. Get ready for its weight.
subtitle: Why the night training came first

row.title: light words
sub: easy to carry, easy to drop

then: Aishah saw sweat on his forehead on a very cold day as revelation ended. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said the heaviness is {idea}acting on it{/idea}. Ibn Zayd added it is heavy in this world and {reward}heavy on the Scales{/reward} on the Day of Judgement.
now: You saved a verse as your lock screen. It looks nice. But living it at work when a colleague takes credit for your project is a different weight. {idea}The words are light to hold and heavy to carry.{/idea}
old: Knowing a verse is the same as carrying it.
new: The Quran is heavy because it asks to be lived, and that weight counts on the Scales.
try: Choose one verse you know well and do one thing today that it asks of you.

title: Night words go straighter into the heart.
subtitle: Why the night hours suit the Quran
then: Umar, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zubayr said every hour of the night counts here. Ibn Kathir explains that standing at night is {idea}better for training the heart and the tongue{/idea}, because the daytime is when people scatter, move about and raise their voices.
now: Daytime: notifications, the school run, a boss on the line, the kettle, the news. Then the house goes quiet after Isha. {reward}The same verse you skimmed at noon suddenly means something at night.{/reward}
old: I will find time for the Quran when the day calms down, which it never does.
new: The calm already exists. It comes every night, made for exactly this.
try: Tonight, after the house is quiet, recite one short surah you know by heart.

title: The day has plenty of room for your affairs.
subtitle: The day is for work, the night is kept
then: The early scholars said Sabh means long free time and activity in the day. Ibn Zayd explained: the day is {idea}for your needs, so leave the night open for devotion{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ had long days of calling people, and the night was kept for his Lord.
now: Work runs from nine to six, then emails at nine pm, then a show, then scrolling until one. {trap}The night gets spent like extra daytime.{/trap} The day already has plenty of room for your affairs.
old: My night is just more hours to finish what the day left over.
new: The day has room for my business, so part of my night can belong to Allah.
try: Pick a cut-off time tonight after which no work messages get answered.

title: Remember His name and turn to Him completely.
subtitle: Devotion after the tasks are done
then: Ibn Kathir explains: make much remembrance of Him, and {idea}devote your time to Him once your worldly tasks are done{/idea}, as in So when you have finished, devote yourself. Ibn Jarir notes the Prophet ﷺ {trap}forbade avoiding marriage{/trap} for worship, so this devotion is not leaving life.
now: The laptop is shut. The kids are asleep. The dishes are done. That small gap before bed is where your mind usually goes to the phone. {idea}It can go to His name instead.{/idea} Devotion fits inside a normal life.
old: Real devotion means giving up my job and family life.
new: Devotion is turning wholly to Him in the time my tasks leave free.
try: When you finish your last task today, say SubhanAllah ten times before picking up your phone.

title: Lord of east and west, so hand Him your affairs.
subtitle: Worship Him alone, rely on Him alone
then: He owns and controls the eastern and western regions, says Ibn Kathir, and none but Him is worthy of worship. {idea}Just as you single Him out for worship, single Him out for reliance.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ was about to carry a mission much bigger than himself.
now: The job application is sent. The scan results come Thursday. Your child is driving across the city alone. {trap}You keep checking, as if your worry holds it together.{/trap} {reward}He is Lord of every road and every horizon.{/reward}
old: If I stop worrying about it, everything will fall apart.
new: I worship the One who runs east and west, so I can hand Him what I cannot hold.
try: Name one worry out loud today and say: I leave this with You, my Trustee.

title: Bear what they say, and step away with grace.
subtitle: A beautiful way to walk away
then: By now the Prophet ﷺ was preaching openly and opposition in Makkah had grown strong. Allah told him to be patient with what the foolish among his people said, and to {idea}keep away from them in a way that is not blameworthy{/idea}.
now: Someone in the family group chat posts another sneering comment about you. You type a long reply, then hover. {idea}You can leave the chat without a parting shot.{/idea} {trap}The clever comeback{/trap} is not the only way to keep your dignity.
old: If I do not answer back, they win.
new: Patience and a graceful exit leave me nothing to regret later.
try: Next time someone provokes you today, delete the reply you drafted and step away politely.

title: Leave the comfortable deniers to Me. Their time is short.
subtitle: Handing the outcome back to Allah
then: Ibn Kathir says this is about {trap}the rich rejectors who owned great wealth{/trap}. They were more able to obey than others, and more was owed from what they had. Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ: leave them to Me, and {idea}give them respite a little{/idea}.
now: Your salary went up. The car is new. Life is comfortable and quiet. {trap}Comfort can make you feel you are already doing fine with Allah.{/trap} {idea}Ease is not a pass. It is a bigger account.{/idea}
old: Things are going well for me, so I must be on the right path.
new: The more ease I have, the more I am able to give and the more I am asked.
try: Look at one comfort you enjoy today and give a small part of it to someone in need.

title: Shackles and fire wait with Allah for the deniers.
subtitle: What awaits the ones who were warned
then: Right after the respite for the comfortable deniers, Allah names what is with Him. A long list of early scholars, including Ibn Abbas, said Ankal means {trap}fetters{/trap}. Those who felt nothing could restrain them in Makkah were told what restraint truly looks like.
now: You tell yourself no one can tell you what to do. Not your parents, not the imam, not a verse. {idea}That freedom is real, and it is short.{/idea} The question is what you do with it while it lasts.
old: Nobody has a right to hold me to anything.
new: My freedom now is a respite, and what I do with it decides what holds me later.
try: Choose one thing you know you should stop doing and freely let it go today.

title: Food that will not go down, and pain.
subtitle: The end of a life of easy pleasure
then: These were the people of ease, enjoying the good things of life. Ibn Abbas explained the food that chokes as food that {trap}gets stuck in the throat and will not go in or out{/trap}. The warning was sent while there was still time to change.
now: Dinner with friends, the third plate, the dessert menu. None of that is wrong in itself. {idea}What matters is whether the blessing ever reminded you of the One who gave it.{/idea} Gratitude turns food into a good deed.
old: What I eat and enjoy has nothing to do with my faith.
new: Every pleasure I am given can be thanked for now, so it does not turn against me later.
try: Before your next meal, say Bismillah slowly, and Alhamdulillah when you finish.

title: The day mountains run like poured sand.
subtitle: When the firmest things stop being firm
then: Ibn Kathir describes the mountains becoming {trap}like hills of sand after they had been firm rocks{/trap}, then utterly gone, until the earth is flat with no valley or hill. The Makkans lived among mountains. Nothing around them looked more permanent.
now: The house you are paying off. The career you have spent fifteen years building. The reputation you guard. {idea}If mountains run like sand, these are not the ground you stand on.{/idea} Allah is.
old: The things I have built will hold me up.
new: Even mountains will pour away, so I lean my weight on the One who does not change.
try: Notice one thing you treat as permanent today and thank Allah for it as a loan.

title: A Messenger sent as a witness over you.
subtitle: Someone who sees what you do with the message

row.title: a witness
sub: sees what you did with it

then: Here Allah addresses the disbelievers of Quraysh, and with them all of mankind. The Messenger ﷺ is {idea}a witness over you, witnessing your deeds{/idea}. They are reminded of another messenger, the one sent to Pharaoh.
now: You have heard the reminder at Friday prayer, in a clip on your feed, from your mother. {idea}A message is not just information. Someone will bear witness to what you did after you heard it.{/idea}
old: I have heard the message, so I have done my part.
new: Hearing it makes me answerable, because the Messenger ﷺ witnesses what I do with it.
try: Recall the last reminder you heard and act on one piece of it today.

title: Pharaoh disobeyed, and was seized with a crushing grip.
subtitle: A past story told as a mirror
then: Ibn Abbas and others said wabil means severe. The message to Quraysh was: {trap}beware of denying this Messenger, lest what befell Pharaoh befall you{/trap}. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid added that their Messenger ﷺ was even greater than Musa.
now: You do not rule an empire. But you might have a little Pharaoh moment: at home, at the office, in a comment thread, refusing to hear correction because you are the one in charge. {idea}The story is about you, not just him.{/idea}
old: The Pharaoh story is about evil rulers long ago.
new: Pharaoh's story warns me about every time I refuse truth because I feel strong.
try: Ask someone you have authority over for one honest piece of feedback, and just listen.

title: A Day that turns children's hair white.
subtitle: How will you protect yourself from it?
then: Ibn Kathir says the hair of children turns grey {trap}from the severity of its horrors{/trap}. He gives two readings: how can you be safe that Day if you disbelieve, or how can you be mindful of Allah if you deny the Day. He calls the first closer to the truth.
now: You have seen a person age ten years in one hard month at a hospital bedside. {idea}Some days change us in a moment.{/idea} This verse asks a simple question while there is time: what will you be holding on to when that Day comes?
old: I will think about the Day of Judgement when I am older.
new: The shelter for that Day is built now, through belief and care in how I live.
try: Make one sincere dua today asking Allah for safety on that Day.

title: Even the sky splits. His promise always comes true.
subtitle: A promise with no way around it
then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah said the sky splits {trap}because of that Day, its severity and its horror{/trap}. Then Allah says His promise is done. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}it will occur, and there is no avoiding it{/idea}.
now: People promise you things all the time. A refund in five working days. A call back. A friend who will be there. Some come, some never do. {idea}Allah's promise is the one that always arrives.{/idea} That is a warning, and a comfort.
old: Promises get broken, so I do not take any of them too seriously.
new: Allah's promise is the one certainty, both His warning and His mercy.
try: Recall one promise of mercy in the Quran and repeat it to yourself today.

title: This is a reminder. Whoever wills, take a road to Him.
subtitle: The door left open after the warning
then: After the warnings, Allah says {idea}this surah is an admonition{/idea} that people of understanding take to heart. Then the door: whoever wills may take a way to his Lord. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse: you cannot will unless Allah wills.
now: You have just read heavy verses and feel the weight. Maybe a little fear. {reward}That feeling is not a closed door. It is a signpost.{/reward} The road to your Lord starts with one step you choose today.
old: After hearing all those warnings, I feel too far gone.
new: The warning is a reminder, and right after it the road to my Lord is held open.
try: Take one small step toward Allah today, and ask Him to make you will it.

title: Your Lord saw you struggle, and made it easy.
subtitle: Mercy after a year of swollen feet
then: Aishah said Allah held back this last part for a year while they stood at night until their feet swelled. Then came the relief: {reward}recite what is easy{/reward}. Allah knew some would be ill, traveling for trade, or striving in His way. Ibn Abbas said: {idea}He made the matter easy, and did not make it difficult{/idea}.
now: Night shifts at the hospital. A newborn who wakes every two hours. A long commute and a body that aches. {reward}Allah knows your exact day.{/reward} He asks what is easy, your prayer, some giving, and a lot of asking forgiveness.
old: If I cannot worship like the people of old, my effort is worthless.
new: Allah sees my real limits and asks what is easy, then multiplies it.
try: Do one easy act today: a few verses, a small donation, and Astaghfirullah before sleep.
